account: Paul Conyngham, a Sydney machine-learning engineer, used ChatGPT to plan treatment for his dog Rosie. Rosie is an eight-year-old Staffy-Shar Pei cross with mast cell cancer diagnosed in 2024. He paid $3,000 for tumor sequencing at UNSW's Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics, and he used AlphaFold to model mutated proteins from the results. He chose neoantigen targets and confirmed them “again using AI”. Pall Thordarson's UNSW RNA Institute made the mRNA vaccine in under two months. Rachel Allavena of the University of Queensland injected it at Gatton in December 2025, with a checkpoint inhibitor, and gave a booster in February 2026. The tennis-ball-sized tumor on Rosie's hock halved, and she was chasing rabbits by late January 2026. Some tumors did not respond. The Verge reported on 18 March 2026 that two outside researchers, David Ascher and Alvin Chan, judged that the AI's role had been overstated. The reporter noted that the checkpoint inhibitor given with the vaccine makes the vaccine's own effect unclear. Medical Daily reported on 18 August 2026 that Rosie had entered remission and that her cancer had returned after a later surgery. According to a 机器之心 report of 24 August 2026, Conyngham wrote on X in June 2026 that the surgery took the cancer out of remission and that he chose to have Rosie euthanized.

ai_role.statement: The AI tools worked at the design stage. ChatGPT suggested immunotherapy, pointed Conyngham to UNSW's genomics center and helped him plan the analysis. AlphaFold modeled mutated proteins. He says he “confirmed, again using AI, that those targets were good cancer candidates”. Humans sequenced the genome (Martin Smith), made the mRNA and nanoparticles (Pall Thordarson) and injected it (Rachel Allavena). A checkpoint inhibitor was given at the same time. UNSW says “We don't know how much of the response came from the checkpoint inhibitor and how much from the mRNA vaccine”. The AI's share of the outcome therefore cannot be isolated. It is a single uncontrolled case, and no outcome data have been published outside interviews and statements.

comparator.quote: Heartbroken when his fur-baby was diagnosed with a deadly mast cell cancer in 2024, Mr ­Conyngham threw thousands of dollars at veterinary chemotherapy and surgery, which slowed but failed to shrink the tumours. Now, after treatment with a custom mRNA cancer vaccine over the Christmas break, the tennis ball-sized tumour on Rosie’s hock has shrunk in half, in a recovery that has astounded researchers at the cutting-edge of human cancer treatments.

He chose neoantigen targets and confirmed them “again using AI”. Pall Thordarson's UNSW RNA Institute made the mRNA vaccine in under two months. Rachel Allavena of the University of Queensland injected it at Gatton in December 2025, with a checkpoint inhibitor, and gave a booster in February 2026. The tennis-ball-sized tumor on Rosie's hock halved, and she was chasing rabbits by late January 2026. Some tumors did not respond. The Verge reported on 18 March 2026 that two outside researchers, David Ascher and Alvin Chan, judged that the AI's role had been overstated. The reporter noted that the checkpoint inhibitor given with the vaccine makes the vaccine's own effect unclear. Medical Daily reported on 18 August 2026 that Rosie had entered remission and that her cancer had returned after a later surgery. According to a 机器之心 report of 24 August 2026, Conyngham wrote on X in June 2026 that the surgery took the cancer out of remission and that he chose to have Rosie euthanized.
